name: uBlock Origin (uBO) and the EasyList filter-list family (EasyList, EasyPrivacy, Peter Lowe's ad-server list, uBO's own uAssets Badware/Privacy/Unbreak lists); plus uBlock Origin Lite (uBOL) under MV3
kind: Browser extension (content blocker) plus a set of community-maintained rule lists. The lists, not the engine, are the interesting object here.
maturity: Production and heavily deployed, but in a forced migration. uBO proper depends on Manifest V2 blocking webRequest and is being displaced in Chromium by uBOL, whose declarativeNetRequest backend cannot express the dynamic and scriptlet behaviour uBO relies on. On Firefox — the platform this project drives — full uBO remains available and supported, which is a material and often-overlooked advantage of the Firefox choice.
license: GPL-3.0 for uBO. EasyList is dual GPLv3 / CC BY-SA 3.0. Both permit use, including in a commercial pipeline, provided modifications to uBO itself would be redistributed under GPL. Merely running the extension imposes no obligation. Vendoring or forking the lists requires attribution and share-alike on the list.
keeps_and_discards: This is the one item in the privacy set that genuinely changes what content survives, which is why it carries a real measured cost here. It discards at three layers: (1) network requests matching filter rules never fire, so any content those requests would have delivered is absent — third-party embeds, comment widgets, video players, social embeds, recommendation rails, and a large share of consent-management scripts; (2) cosmetic filters (##selector) remove matched elements from the DOM after parse; (3) scriptlet injections (##+js(...)) neuter specific page scripts. Layers 2 and 3 are the ones that matter constitutionally: cosmetic filters are CSS-selector rules that name page regions, which is a structure classifier in everything but name.
structure_preserved: Nesting and ordering of what remains are exact — uBO does not rewrite the tree, it deletes subtrees. Tabular relations survive unless a cosmetic rule happens to cut inside a table. Shadow boundaries: uBO's cosmetic filtering has limited and evolving reach into shadow DOM and none into closed roots, so a page whose ads live inside a closed root is unfiltered — the same blindness this project accepts by policy, arrived at by accident. The specific structural hazard is that a cosmetic rule removes a node the fold would otherwise address, so an xpath-keyed trie sees a deletion that has no corresponding page-authored mutation.
interactive_elements: Controls inside blocked or cosmetically-removed subtrees disappear entirely. Controls whose initialisation depended on a blocked script remain in the DOM as inert markup. Both outcomes are directly relevant to the local measurement that the projection draws 80.9% of the affordances a page offers against 99.7% held at capture: tracker blocking is a plausible contributor to affordance loss on live sites, and it is testable by comparing the affordance ratio across the existing blocked and unblocked arms.
interactive_state_fidelity: Where content survives, state fidelity is exact — uBO does not touch attributes on surviving nodes, so disabled / checked / selected / aria-expanded and the ARIA surface are whatever the page set, at zero token cost. The damage is categorical rather than gradual: an affected control is gone or inert, not degraded. The inert case is the dangerous one and it is silent — an element carrying aria-expanded="false" whose expand handler was blocked looks identical to a genuinely collapsed control, so the fold records a state that can never change. Distinguishing 'collapsed' from 'collapsed and broken' is not possible from tag-plus-interactivity alone. [uncertain] No published measurement of ARIA-state divergence under blocking exists; the local blocked-versus-unblocked arms could measure it directly.
layout_awareness: The network layer reads no geometry. Cosmetic filtering reads the DOM and CSS selectors but not computed geometry, with one exception: uBO supports procedural cosmetic operators (:has, :has-text, :matches-css, :xpath, :upward, :others) and :matches-css does consult computed style. So a small slice of the cosmetic layer is style-aware, and none of it is layout-aware in the getBoundingClientRect sense.
javascript_required: Blocking happens with or without page scripts, but its POINT is to prevent scripts running. This is the only mechanism in the privacy set that materially reduces whether telemetry fires rather than only what it learns — which is exactly why it costs 10.49% on live sites and only 0.16% on saved pages in the local measurement. That 65x gap is the signature of a request-suppressing defense: on a saved page most requests are already unreachable, so the blocker has almost nothing left to suppress and the residual 0.16% is cosmetic filtering plus the 0.07% null-control floor.
evaluation_method: There is no systematic evaluation. Effectiveness is asserted by list coverage and measured episodically by third-party ad-blocker comparisons of varying quality. Breakage is evaluated by issue report: the uAssets and uBlock-issues trackers are the de facto test suite, and the 'Unbreak' list exists precisely as an accumulated record of past false positives. uBO's own documentation states the trade-off qualitatively — probability of page breakage rises with the number of enabled lists — without quantifying it.
corpus_size_and_origins: No fixed corpus for either effectiveness or breakage, in the entire history of the project. Breakage evidence is an unbounded, self-selected complaint stream biased toward sites people care about. Academic tracker-prevalence measurements (Tranco-based crawls of top-N sites) measure what filter lists catch on a ranked head sample and generalise poorly to the tail. Nothing here is frozen; no breakage rate quoted for uBO has a stable denominator. This is a notably weaker evidence base than the 136-page/109-origin local corpus, small as that is.
reported_precision_recall: No published precision/recall against a labelled ground truth of trackers, because no such ground truth exists at scale. Coverage claims are list-size claims. The one metric this project already holds is far more useful than anything published: 10.49% fold drift on live sites and 0.16% on saved pages, against a 0.07% null-control floor. That is a measured recall cost with an explicit denominator, which is more than the ad-blocking literature offers.
independent_oracle: Weak and partly circular. The usual oracle for 'did blocking work' is another filter list or a tracker-detection heuristic that shares the same assumptions about what a tracker is. Genuinely independent checks exist for the cost side rather than the benefit side: comparing captured content with and without blocking, which is exactly the local blocked/unblocked arm design. That arm is a better oracle for this project's purposes than anything in the literature.
evidence_independence: Effectiveness claims are first-party (uBO maintainers, list maintainers) or come from ad-blocker vendors comparing themselves. Breakage evidence is crowd-sourced. Academic prevalence studies are independent but measure tracker presence, not blocker fidelity cost. There is no vendor-neutral fidelity comparison.
page_archetype_coverage: Highly uneven and predictable from mechanism. Documentation and article pages lose little because their content is first-party. Forum and collection pages lose embedded media, avatars served from CDNs on blocklists, and comment systems. Product and listing pages lose recommendation rails, review widgets and image CDNs, which is real content loss rather than noise removal. Service pages are the worst case, because blocking can break login flows, payment widgets and consent interfaces outright. Any single aggregate cost figure across archetypes is misleading in the same way WCXB's 0.93-to-0.41 spread is; the local 10.49% should be reported per archetype before it is trusted as a single number. [uncertain]
script_and_locale_behaviour: The lists are heavily Anglophone-and-European in origin, with regional supplements (RU, CN, JP, DE, FR and others) maintained at uneven quality. Coverage on non-Western sites is therefore inconsistent, which means the fidelity cost of blocking is itself locale-dependent — a multilingual corpus will show a different cost per language, and that difference is a property of the list, not of the page. Text handling is script-invariant: uBO removes nodes, it does not transform text, so CJK, RTL and whitespace-free segmentation are unaffected in what survives.
leaks_outward: Substantially reduces outward disclosure, and this is its principal value here. Against the measured local baseline of roughly 3,082 external requests per corpus run to 92+ distinct hosts, EasyPrivacy plus EasyList would suppress a large fraction — that number is exactly the metric a blocking arm should be scored on, alongside the 10.49% fidelity cost. The correct framing is a two-axis trade the project can already measure: requests-suppressed against fold-drift-incurred. No other item in this set lets both axes be measured against a null control.
mechanism_detectability: Detectable and actively detected in production, by multiple deployed mechanisms. The concrete signals: (1) bait-element probing — a page inserts a decoy node with a class name matching a known EasyList cosmetic rule and checks whether it was removed or whether its computed height is zero; this is the classic anti-adblock test and is deployed today by Admiral, BlockThrough and the major publisher anti-adblock vendors; (2) failed-request probing — issuing a fetch to a known blocked ad host and observing the error; (3) scriptlet-artifact probing — uBO's ##+js scriptlets replace page functions with stubs whose toString or property descriptors differ from native, which is directly checkable; (4) extension-presence probing via web-accessible resources, largely mitigated in modern uBO but historically effective. Blocking is therefore a LOUD choice: it converts the session from 'ordinary visitor' to 'visitor running a content blocker', and on anti-adblock-defended sites it triggers overlay walls that themselves become the captured content. For this project's stated detectability tension, this ranks blocking as more conspicuous than navigator.webdriver on the subset of sites that run anti-adblock, and less conspicuous on the rest.
countermeasures: Per-site disabling; uBO's own anti-anti-adblock scriptlets (an arms race, not a solution); using EasyPrivacy alone without EasyList, which suppresses trackers while leaving the ad-bait surface that anti-adblock probes target largely intact — this is the highest-value configuration for a capture pipeline and is materially less detectable than the default bundle. The generic countermeasure of 'fewer lists' also directly reduces breakage, per uBO's own guidance.
measured_fidelity_cost: Measured locally and this is the strongest number in the entire privacy set: 10.49% fold drift on live sites, 0.16% on saved pages, against a 0.07% null-control floor. Read carefully, that says the cosmetic-and-scriptlet layer costs about 0.09% above the noise floor (0.16 minus 0.07) while the request-suppression layer costs about 10.3%. Those are two different mechanisms with two different verdicts, and collapsing them into one 10.49% figure hides the finding. The actionable inference: cosmetic filtering is nearly free in fidelity terms and expensive in constitutional terms (it is a structure classifier), while network blocking is expensive in fidelity terms and constitutionally clean (it names hosts, not regions). The project's constraints and its measurements point in opposite directions here, which is worth stating explicitly.
gate_state_at_capture: Blocking materially changes gate incidence in BOTH directions and records nothing about it, which makes it the single largest silent-bias risk in this set. It suppresses many consent-management scripts, so a page that would have shown a consent interface renders without one — the capture looks ungated and is not. It also triggers anti-adblock walls on defended sites, adding a gate that would not otherwise exist. With roughly 67% of top sites presenting a consent interface, a corpus captured with blocking on and gate state unrecorded is not comparable to one captured with it off, and the difference is not noise. Gate state must be recorded from positive evidence per capture.
determinism: Deterministic given a pinned list version and a pinned page: the same rules match the same requests and the same selectors. In practice non-deterministic, because lists auto-update on a schedule (typically daily) and because cosmetic filtering races page script — a rule can apply before or after a script inserts a node, producing run-to-run differences on dynamic pages.
determinism_across_versions: Poor and continuously drifting by design. EasyList changes many times per day; uBO's engine, its procedural-operator set and its scriptlet library change per release; and the MV2-to-MV3 transition changes the expressible rule set outright on Chromium. Any fidelity figure is valid only for a pinned (uBO version, list snapshot) pair, and that pair must be recorded with the measurement. A 10.49% figure measured six months apart is not the same measurement.
reproducibility: Requires pinning the list snapshots, not merely the extension version — which is the step almost every published comparison omits. uBO supports importing local list files, so pinning is mechanically easy and should be treated as mandatory for any measured arm. The local corpus's own instability (75% of pages fetch live resources on every read) compounds this: with both the lists and the pages moving, a re-run measures two drifts at once.
failure_modes: False-positive blocks removing first-party content; cosmetic rules cutting a node the fold needed; scripts left half-initialised after a dependency was blocked; anti-adblock walls replacing the page; login, payment and consent flows broken; and list-update-induced regressions appearing without any change on the capture side.
failure_visibility: Predominantly silent, and this is the disqualifying property for a measured path. A cosmetically-filtered page is well-formed and plausible; a page missing its recommendation rail is well-formed and plausible; a suppressed consent banner is well-formed, plausible, and biasing. uBO surfaces a per-tab block count, which is a coarse loudness signal that a pipeline COULD read and record — capturing that count per page is the cheapest available honesty measure and turns a silent degradation into a recorded one.
scale_limits: Filter-list compilation and memory are the cost, and they are roughly linear in rule count with a fixed per-tab overhead for cosmetic filtering. Procedural cosmetic operators (:has-text, :matches-css, :upward) are evaluated repeatedly against DOM mutations and are markedly more expensive than plain selectors on mutation-heavy pages — this is the one place uBO's cost becomes superlinear in page activity rather than page size, and it is directly relevant to a project already fighting superlinear ingest.
delta_cost_model: No formal model, and a specific and serious interaction with an O(delta) design. Procedural cosmetic filtering re-evaluates on DOM mutation, and cosmetic removals are themselves DOM mutations — so a blocker running inside the same page as a mutation-driven sensor creates a feedback surface: page mutation triggers filter re-evaluation triggers node removal triggers another mutation record. The sensor will observe deletions with no page-authored cause. Two changes fall outside any naive delta model here: list auto-updates (which change what is removed with zero page change) and CSS-driven cosmetic hiding (::style rules that hide without removing, producing no mutation record at all).
reanchoring_stability: Actively harmful to xpath-keyed anchoring. Cosmetic removal deletes intermediate nodes, which shifts positional xpath indices for every following sibling — so a single blocked ad slot can invalidate the addresses of an entire sibling run. Content-hash and CDC-boundary anchors survive this; raw positional xpath does not. If the trie key is url:xpath, enabling cosmetic filtering will inflate the re-anchor rate for reasons unrelated to page change, and worse, the inflation will vary with list updates. This argues for keeping cosmetic filtering off in any arm where re-anchor rate is being measured. [uncertain] No published re-anchor-rate measurement under blocking exists; the local arms could measure it.
adversarial_exposure: Modestly helpful, incidentally, and not in a way that can be relied on. Blocking removes third-party-delivered content, and third-party ad and widget slots are one delivery path for injected instructions — so some injected content never arrives. It does nothing about first-party concealment, which is the dominant case: the 2026 in-the-wild census puts roughly 70% of injections in non-rendered first-party HTML (HTTP headers, comments, JSON-LD, meta) and 58.6% of reachable HTML-embedded ones behind rendering-based concealment, none of which a network blocker touches. Treat the adversarial benefit as a rounding error, not a defense.
provenance_carrying: None in the representation. Two capture-envelope facts are essential and easy to record: the pinned list snapshot identifiers, and uBO's per-tab block count. Without the first, a fidelity number is uninterpretable; without the second, absent content cannot be attributed to blocking rather than to the page.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable; uBO performs no serialisation, no escaping and no text normalisation. It deletes nodes and drops requests.
token_budget_and_ordering: Indirect but real: blocking reduces tokens per page by removing third-party content, and the removed content is disproportionately low-value boilerplate (ad slots, tracking pixels, social embeds). That is the one genuinely favourable slm_interface property in this item — the tokens it saves are usually tokens worth losing. It imposes no ordering policy. The caution is that the 10.49% fold drift on live sites is not all boilerplate; some fraction is product imagery, reviews and embedded media that a downstream task may need.
representation_cost: Reduces tokens per page by an unmeasured amount that should be measured alongside the fidelity cost. Tokens-saved against fidelity-lost is the right ratio, and this project can compute both from the arms it already runs. [uncertain]
what_could_be_adopted: Split the item in two, because the two halves get opposite verdicts and the project's own measurements make the split empirically as well as constitutionally. The NETWORK layer — EasyPrivacy, host-and-URL-pattern rules — is adoptable in the actuator layer: it names hosts, never page regions, so it is structure-agnostic; it is the only mechanism here that materially reduces the 3,082-requests-to-92-hosts outward leak; and its cost (about 10.3% of the 10.49%) is measured, bounded and attributable. Recommended configuration is EasyPrivacy alone, pinned to a snapshot, with the per-tab block count recorded per capture and gate state recorded from positive evidence. The COSMETIC and SCRIPTLET layers should be rejected: they are CSS-selector rule lists that name page regions, which is a structure classifier by definition; they corrupt positional-xpath anchoring; they create a mutation feedback loop against an O(delta) sensor; and — the decisive point — they buy almost nothing, costing only about 0.09% above the null-control floor on saved pages, which means their entire fidelity contribution is negligible while their constitutional cost is total. Separately, uBO's own documented finding that breakage probability rises with list count is a directly transferable operating rule: fewer lists, pinned, is strictly better here than comprehensive coverage.

constraint_violation_ledger.verdict: Split verdict. Network-layer blocking (EasyPrivacy, host/URL rules): adoptable in the actuator layer only. Cosmetic filtering and scriptlet injection: rejected. As a whole-bundle default: rejected.
constraint_violation_ledger.structure_agnosticism: Network layer: no conflict, it matches hosts and URL patterns, never page regions. Cosmetic layer: direct violation — ##selector rules are precisely a pre-computed heuristic naming page regions, and procedural operators like :has-text and :upward are region classifiers with extra steps. This is the clearest instance in the whole research set of a widely-deployed practical mechanism that the structure_agnosticism constraint forbids outright.
constraint_violation_ledger.no_layout_in_the_fold: Network layer: no conflict. Cosmetic layer: mostly compatible in letter (selectors, not geometry) but :matches-css consults computed style, which imports a style read into a filtering decision. Minor violation, and avoidable by excluding procedural rules.
constraint_violation_ledger.o_delta: Violation in the cosmetic layer: filter-driven node removal generates mutation records with no page-authored cause, procedural rules re-evaluate on every mutation (superlinear in page activity), and list auto-updates change output with zero page change — a change entirely outside the delta model. Network layer is delta-neutral.
constraint_violation_ledger.no_mocks: Compatible in the sense that it runs in a real browser with real page scripts, but blocking makes the captured page a materially different artifact from the served one — 10.49% different on live sites, measured. That is not a stub, but it is a systematic divergence that must be declared as an arm rather than enabled by default in a measured path.
constraint_violation_ledger.closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: Fully consistent, by accident rather than principle: uBO's cosmetic filtering has limited reach into open shadow DOM and none into closed roots, and it does not patch attachShadow. It arrives at the project's policy for engineering reasons, which is mild independent support for that policy being the practical norm.

governance_signal_handling: None, and there is a real tension worth naming. uBO reads no robots.txt and has no AIPREF, Content Signals, ai.txt, Web Bot Auth or HTTP 402 awareness. More pointedly, blocking is adversarial to the site's expressed commercial preference in a way the emerging governance stack is designed to formalise: the same publishers now deploying Content Signals and HTTP 402 pay-per-crawl are the ones deploying anti-adblock. A pipeline that both blocks trackers and claims to honour Content Signals is taking a coherent legal position but an incoherent behavioural one, and defended sites will detect the mismatch before any standard adjudicates it.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Blocking is defensively useful under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 but does not change the regulated act. Its genuine value is data minimisation on the capture path — suppressing third-party requests means the operator's browsing is not itself broadcast to 92+ hosts per run, which is a real reduction in processing the controller causes. It has a second, more direct benefit: blocked third-party embeds are a common carrier of other people's personal data (social widgets, comment systems, user avatars), so blocking reduces the PII incidentally captured into stored artifacts. That is a genuine minimisation argument for the network layer specifically, and it is worth making explicitly if legitimate interest is ever relied on.
